newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai central banker leaves amid finance turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Thai central banker leaves amid finance turmoil.

text.p: Outgoing Thai central bank head Rerngchai Marakanond leaves his post on Tuesday after a tumultuous year in office during which he was perceived as failing to do enough to help the country's battered economy.

Rerngchai, a 25-year central bank veteran, tendered his resignation amid criticism that the Bank of Thailand had been ill prepared to handle the flotation of the baht and did not do enough to solve the problems facing the ailing finance sector.
Government sources said Rerngchai had attempted to resign several times before but his offer had not been accepted.

Rerngchai unexpectedly submitted his resignation late on Monday, just as Thailand said it would accept advice from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and possible IMF aid to try to revive the economy, which is languishing at 10-year lows.

The governor, who took office last July after former Bank of Thailand governor Vijit Supinit quit following a series of scandals, had originally been welcomed by the finance community as a conservative figure who could ensure stability.

But he was beset by continual problems, especially after the change of premier Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's government in November last year. Chavalit had made solving economic problems as a top priority for his administration.

Rerngchai was criticised after the government's decision to put the baht into a managed float after it had been pegged to a basket of currencies for 13 years. Analysts said the central bank was not fully prepared for the fallout from the float.
The bank spent millions of dollars after the float to defend the currency, which has lost about 20 percent of its value since July 2.

Rerngchai was also under pressure for his handling of troubles in the ailing financial sector, and the central bank has come under fire for keeping interest rates high in defence of the embattled baht.
The front-runner to replace Rerngchai is his deputy, Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi.

Analysts said the 50-year old banker, who holds a doctorate from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), would face a tough challenge to stabilise the economy and bring confidence back to the currency.
